summary.text: 车 is a modern simplified form of 車, a pictograph of a wheeled vehicle. Its shape derives from the traditional graph’s cursive form.

formation.text: The traditional graph 車 pictures a vehicle as a whole. Early forms varied in the features shown; later forms selected and regularized some of them. The modern graph 车 derives from cursive 車.

history.text: Early oracle-bone and bronze forms of 車 varied in the vehicle features shown. Later forms selected and regularized some features. The curated oracle-bone, Western Zhou bronze, and seal-script examples illustrate different presentations; they are modern redrawings, not artifact photographs.
The modern simplified form 车 derives from cursive 車, attested by the Sui dynasty at the latest. It became a standard character in 1956. This change is distinct from earlier variation within 車.

uncertainties.text: Early forms varied, and the curated images are modern redrawings. Individual vehicle features in any one drawing should therefore be interpreted cautiously.
Early vehicle uses are identified by inscription references, but the cited evidence gives neither calendar dates for those inscriptions nor a precise earliest date for the graph.

senses.text: Oracle-bone examples use 車 for vehicles, and bronze examples include vehicles and war chariots. These attest early vehicle-related use but do not establish a calendar-dated first occurrence.
An oracle-bone example is identified as a place-name use. Its meaning and any connection to the vehicle sense are unresolved.

senses.gloss: wheeled machines; transporting by cart; cartload measure
senses.text: Later dictionaries record these uses, but the evidence does not date their emergence or establish a continuous development from the vehicle sense.
The common modern meaning includes vehicle and car.

limitations.text: The chronology and semantic links among later machinery, transport, and measure senses are unresolved, so no chain of development is proposed.

Some proposals treat the spoken word written 車 as borrowed from Indo-Iranian words for “wheel” or “chariot.” In that account, the graph was reused for another word because the words sounded alike or similar; the vehicle picture did not develop into that word’s meaning. The depicted vehicle’s spoken name is not independently established, so the proposed sound match remains disputed.
The traditional account that Xi Zhong made the vehicle in the Xia period is not independently confirmed by the cited evidence.

overview.text: 车 is the simplified form of 車, whose early forms pictured a wheeled vehicle. The modern shape comes from cursive writing of the traditional character.

Pictogram (象形) – originally a carriage seen from above. In the oracle bone script, there were large wheels on both sides and a central shaft at the front.
Unrelated to 倝 and 朝.
Perhaps a loan from an Indo-European language because the horse and chariot were introduced into China around 1200 BC from Inner Asia; compare Tocharian A kukäl, Tocharian B kokale (“wagon; cart”) (Mair, 1990, Bauer, 1994), from Proto-Tocharian *kuk(ä)le, from Proto-Indo-European *kʷékʷlos, a form of *kʷel- (“to turn”). Cognate with English wheel, Ancient Greek κύκλος (kúklos), Lithuanian kaklas (“neck”), etc.
Sagart and Baxter (2025) specifically pinpoint descent from some reflex of Proto-Indo-Iranian *čakrám and update their 2014 reconstructions to *t.[qʰ]rA > chē and *[C.q]ra > jū. They also suppose that the variation of pronunciations could be attributed to separate borrowing events from Indo-Aryan and Iranian.
An older variant survives in Mandarin 軲轆／轱辘 (gūlu, “wheel”) (Bauer, 1994). Alternatively, the word is a derivation by k-prefix from 舁 (OC *la, “to lift”) (Baxter and Sagart, 1998); compare the semantic parallel in Tibetan ཐེག་པ (theg pa, “vehicle; carriage”) (OC *kʰljaʔ, *kʰljas) and 居 (OC *kas) (Schuessler, 2007). Pronunciation 2 is traditionally regarded as the older pronunciation.
The sense of lewd content is derived from 老司機 /老司机 (lǎosījī).

Etymological analysis: pictographic

The database describes Shang oracle-bone forms as variable, sometimes depicting wheels, carriage body, axle, yoke, pole and crossbar; later forms retain selected features, producing the regular 車 form. It lists oracle-bone, bronze, Chu manuscript and seal-script evidence. This supports a pictorial graph, with reduction and stylization over time.
evidence.title: 漢字「車」：字形演變

evidence.source: Chinese University of Hong Kong, Multi-function Chinese Character Database
evidence.field: traditional 車 forms and early uses
evidence.text: The database says oracle-bone and bronze forms vary and may depict the vehicle’s wheels, body, axle, yoke, pole and crossbar. It reports an oracle-bone use for a vehicle in Heji 11452 (“six vehicles”), another in Heji 11450 (“vehicles and horses”), and a place-name use in Heji 584. Bronze inscriptions use 車 for vehicles and also for war chariots. These are source-reported inscription readings; the supplied page does not give calendar dates for each quoted inscription.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫 — 車

evidence.text: The page distinguishes complex and simplified variants already present in Shang and Western Zhou writing, including complex and simpler forms in adjacent columns of the same Western Zhou inscription. It says the simpler 車 form had become the sole common form by the Eastern Zhou. This is a historical account of graphic variants, distinct from the much later modern simplified character 车.
evidence.title: 从单个字符形体的简化看字形与繁简关系

evidence.text: The author identifies 车 as a cursive form of 車, attested by the Sui dynasty at the latest and continuing in later cursive writing, but says it did not become generally used as a standard character until adoption in the first simplified-character list. The formal 1956 reform resolution states that the first table of 230 simplified characters was to be used from 1 February 1956; the 1964 table lists 车 as a simplified component corresponding to 車. These records support the relationship, but do not show the calligraphic exemplars themselves on the inspected page.
evidence.title: 从单个字符形体的简化看字形与繁简关系

evidence.field: traditional 車 definition and historical account
evidence.text: The entry defines 車 as the general name for carriage body and wheels, calls it pictographic, and repeats the traditional claim that Xi Zhong made it in the Xia period. Duan Yucai’s annotation explains the graph as depicting a body, two wheels and an axle, while challenging the claim that Xi Zhong was the first inventor. Treat the Xia attribution as a transmitted historical account, not independent confirmation.
evidence.title: 說文解字「車」

evidence.source: Taiwan Ministry of Education, Dictionary of Chinese Character Variants
evidence.text: The dictionary records chē (ㄔㄜ) and jū (ㄐㄩ). It cites the basic vehicle sense and later extensions to wheeled machines, transporting by cart, a measure for cartloads, and the chess rook reading. It quotes examples from the Han shu, Nan shi, Tang, Song, Ming and Qing texts; these establish cited later uses, not the chronology of every semantic extension. Its entry gives 尺遮切 from Shuowen and lists Guangyun and Jiyun materials, including separate fish- and ma-rhyme entries.
evidence.title: [A04061] 車 — 教育部《異體字字典》

evidence.source: Taiwan Ministry of Education, Revised Mandarin Chinese Dictionary
evidence.text: The entry gives the standard Mandarin reading chē and describes vehicles, rotating machinery, machine sewing or cutting, and a measure for cartloads; it also lists jū as another reading. This is modern lexicographic evidence, not a dated account of when each sense arose.
evidence.title: 《國語辭典簡編本》：車

evidence.source: Wiktionary, citing Baxter–Sagart historical phonology data
evidence.text: For the two readings, the page reports Mandarin chē with Middle Chinese tsyhae and Baxter–Sagart Old Chinese *[t.qʰ](r)A, and Mandarin jū with Middle Chinese kjo and *C.q(r)a in the 2014 Baxter–Sagart system. Its table distinguishes two pronunciations of 車, not phonetic components within the graph. The page also reports Zhengzhang Old Chinese *kʰlja for chē and *kla for jū; these are a separate reconstruction system and should not be merged with Baxter–Sagart forms.
evidence.title: 車 — Wiktionary

evidence.field: modern simplified 车 and modern Mandarin readings
evidence.text: The entry lists chē and jū and describes 车 as adapted from the cursive form of traditional 車. This is a secondary summary; the more detailed Sui-and-later chronology is reported separately by the Beijing Normal University study.
evidence.title: 车 — Dong Chinese dictionary

evidence.text: Bauer’s 1994 comparison shows substantial variation among then-published reconstructions for the word 車, including forms around *khlja, *kalja and *k(r)ja. This reinforces that reconstructed sound forms depend on system and period; it does not establish a loan source or the original spoken name of the depicted vehicle.
evidence.title: Sino-Tibetan *kolo ‘Wheel’

evidence.field: proposed Indo-Iranian comparison: source word and vehicle history
evidence.text: The entry describes Indo-Iranian chariot traditions and the Iranian word čaxra- and Old Indian cakrá- for “wheel,” related to Indo-European *kʷékʷlo-. It reports datable Indo-Aryan chariot-racing terms in the Hittite Kikkuli treatise from the 14th century BCE, while noting that Avestan material cannot be precisely dated. This independently establishes relevant source-language vocabulary and chariot context, but not a borrowing into Chinese or the name of the object pictured by 車.
evidence.title: CHARIOT — Encyclopaedia Iranica

evidence.source: Victor Mair, Robert S. Bauer, and later discussion as summarized in S. V. Shaughnessy, Sino-Platonic Papers
evidence.text: The inspected account attributes to Mair a proposal that Chinese 車 was borrowed from a Proto-Iranian form *caxra- “wheel,” and describes Bauer’s subsequent comparison of Chinese and Bodic wheel terms. A separate current Wiktionary entry reports a newer Sagart–Baxter (2025) proposal connecting Chinese readings to reflexes of Proto-Indo-Iranian *čakrám and suggests separate borrowing histories for chē and jū. These are proposals about the spoken word represented by the whole graph, not about a phonetic component; no inspected primary publication here verifies either derivation. The source object’s name is reconstructed, not directly recoverable from the Chinese pictograph, so graphic resemblance and the pronoun alone do not prove borrowing.
evidence.title: Wheeled Vehicles in the Chinese Bronze Age (c. 2000–741 B.C.)

evidence.source: Wikisource transcription of the State Council resolution
evidence.text: The transcribed resolution is dated 28 January 1956 and states the first table of 230 simplified characters was to be used in printed and handwritten documents from 1 February 1956. Its appendix lists 车（車） among the simplified components. This dates standardization, not the earlier cursive form’s origin.
evidence.title: 汉字简化方案 — 国务院关于公布汉字简化方案的决议

evidence.text: The entry describes Indo-Iranian chariot traditions and the Iranian word čaxra- and Old Indian cakrá- for “wheel,” related to Indo-European *kʷékʷlo-. It reports datable Indo-Aryan chariot-racing terms in the Hittite Kikkuli treatise from the 14th century BCE, while noting that Avestan material cannot be precisely dated. This independently establishes relevant source-language vocabulary and chariot context, but not a borrowing into Chinese or the name of the object pictured by 車.
evidence.title: CHARIOT — Encyclopaedia Iranica

evidence.source: Victor Mair, Robert S. Bauer, and later discussion as summarized in S. V. Shaughnessy, Sino-Platonic Papers
evidence.text: The inspected account attributes to Mair a proposal that Chinese 車 was borrowed from a Proto-Iranian form *caxra- “wheel,” and describes Bauer’s subsequent comparison of Chinese and Bodic wheel terms. A separate current Wiktionary entry reports a newer Sagart–Baxter (2025) proposal connecting Chinese readings to reflexes of Proto-Indo-Iranian *čakrám and suggests separate borrowing histories for chē and jū. These are proposals about the spoken word represented by the whole graph, not about a phonetic component; no inspected primary publication here verifies either derivation. The source object’s name is reconstructed, not directly recoverable from the Chinese pictograph, so graphic resemblance and the pronoun alone do not prove borrowing.
evidence.title: Wheeled Vehicles in the Chinese Bronze Age (c. 2000–741 B.C.)

evidence.source: Wikisource transcription of the State Council resolution
evidence.text: The transcribed resolution is dated 28 January 1956 and states the first table of 230 simplified characters was to be used in printed and handwritten documents from 1 February 1956. Its appendix lists 车（車） among the simplified components. This dates standardization, not the earlier cursive form’s origin.
evidence.title: 汉字简化方案 — 国务院关于公布汉字简化方案的决议

evidence.text: Describes Shang oracle forms as variable, with detailed and abbreviated depictions of vehicle features including wheels, body/frame, crossbar, and yoke; says later writing selected some features to form regular 車. Its page displays oracle-bone, bronze, Chu manuscript, and seal-script categories. This supports pictographic formation and graphic reduction, without implying every version includes every named part.
evidence.title: 漢字「車」：字形演變

evidence.source: Chinese University of Hong Kong, Multi-function Chinese Character Database
evidence.text: Reports variable oracle-bone and bronze forms depicting vehicle features, and that bronze forms are often written vertically. It identifies oracle-bone examples for vehicle use in Heji 11452 (“six vehicles”), vehicle-and-horse use in Heji 11450, and a place-name use in Heji 584. It reports bronze vehicle and war-chariot uses, and later Warring States bamboo-slip vehicle and chariot-punishment uses. These are inscription identifiers and source interpretations; the inspected page does not supply calendar dates for each.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫 — 車

evidence.field: graphic variants and dated bronze exemplars
evidence.text: Lists oracle-bone examples by corpus references and bronze examples with period labels, including late Shang and Western Zhou. The page’s interpretation describes oracle forms with differing combinations of canopy, axle, wheels and vehicle body, and later verticalized forms. It classifies the graph as pictographic. This is a secondary reference and its detailed part-by-part interpretation is not independently demonstrated by the page.
evidence.title: 車字形演变字源_汉字「車」_車的甲骨文_車的金文_金文编_甲骨文编

context.provenance: Base evidence consists of imported local JSONL excerpts. Source names identify upstream datasets; extraction may lose sense and language boundaries. Further external evidence and research activity are documented separately in the dossier.
editorial_rules: Write about the character's graphic history; distinguish it from the history of a spoken word.
Separate historical explanation from mnemonics. Do not infer history from modern shapes or readings.
Sources may repeat one another. A source count is not independent corroboration.
Treat Shuowen as a historical account, not automatic confirmation. Its generated English glosses are excluded.
Unrelated word senses may appear in Wiktionary excerpts. Do not merge them into a character origin.
Related-character evidence retains its record_character. Do not silently transfer a traditional form's components to a simplified form.
No glyph image has been visually inspected in this packet. Do not claim to have inspected one.
Explain missing evidence explicitly, especially for Japanese-created characters. A Chinese spelling pronunciation is not evidence for a Japanese origin.

gaps: The earliest vehicle uses are reported from oracle-bone inscriptions by identifiers Heji 11452 and 11450, but the inspected page does not date those individual inscriptions more precisely.

Later semantic development is not a simple dated sequence: the sources attest vehicle, war-chariot, machinery, transport-by-cart and other senses, but do not establish when each extension first arose or the links between them.

The 2025 Sagart–Baxter proposal was available here only through a secondary character-entry summary; its primary argument and comparative data were not inspected. Older loan proposals and internal derivation accounts remain disputed.

The proposed loan concerns the whole spoken word represented by 車. No independently established name or pronunciation for the depicted vehicle is recoverable from the graph alone; a pronoun reconstruction does not demonstrate the object-name match.

車 is pictographic rather than a phonetic compound, so no semantic/phonetic component pair or component pronunciation comparison applies. No component’s phonetic role should be inferred from the separate whole-word loan proposals.
No visually inspected glyph images are claimed. The paleographic conclusions rely on textual descriptions and databases’ classifications.
No calendar date for the individual oracle-bone examples Heji 11452, 11450, or 584 was given on the inspected CUHK page.
The page supports vehicle and war-chariot senses in early inscriptions, but it does not establish a dated sequence or semantic links for later machine, transport, or measure senses.
The inspected external sources support 車 as pictographic. No semantic/phonetic component pair applies, and no component pronunciation comparison is relevant.

Whole-word loan proposals in the dossier were not reverified in this pass. The original depicted vehicle’s spoken name is not established from its pictograph; reconstructed Chinese pronunciation alone would not prove borrowing from a proposed external vehicle term.

items.tradition: Chinese oracle-bone script; modern vector redraw based on cited Hanziyuan and Academia Sinica character images
items.caption: An oracle-bone style form of 車 has a long central shaft crossed by a bar, with a vehicle body and wheel-like shapes below. Early forms varied in which vehicle features they showed.
items.alt: Black oracle-bone style character with a vertical central stroke, a broad crossbar, and a lower section containing several openings.
items.selection_reason: Provides a clear early pictorial example consistent with descriptions of variable vehicle features in oracle-bone forms.
items.rights: CC0 / public-domain dedication stated on the Commons page.

items.tradition: Chinese bronze-inscription script; modern vector redraw keyed to the cited 同卣 inscription image
items.caption: This Western Zhou bronze-script form of 車 has a crossbar above a framed middle section divided into openings, with a long vertical stroke continuing below.
items.alt: Black bronze-script character with a crossbar, a box-like middle divided into four openings, and a long vertical stroke.
items.selection_reason: Shows a distinct bronze-inscription form that helps illustrate the graph’s changing visual presentation; its specific inscription association is identified as a modern redraw.
items.rights: CC0 / public-domain dedication stated on the Commons page.

items.period: Shuowen seal-script tradition; transmitted dictionary form, compiled c. 100 CE
items.tradition: Chinese seal script; modern vector redraw referencing Hanziyuan and Academia Sinica
items.caption: The seal-script form associated with the Shuowen tradition has a regular framed center crossed by horizontal strokes, with a vertical line extending above and below.
items.alt: Black seal-script character with a rectangular center, horizontal crossbars, and a vertical stroke extending past both ends.
items.selection_reason: Adds a legible seal-script example of the pictographic graph in a regularized form.
items.rights: Public-domain dedication stated on the Commons page.
